entry.description: Chooses always/never/impossible options when the text is measured.
entry.childHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
entry.approvalNote: Cleared on the printed review pack; returned marked up.

textProvenance.note: Ruled when written; absent from the store until now (R403/R410).

stem.text: In lines 11 to 14 the writer repeats words like 'scraped' and 'scrabbled'. Why does he do this?

carriers.key: To show the climb went on and on and was hard work.

options.value: To show that digging is the easiest job a mole ever does.
options.execution: 'The easiest job a mole ever does' overstates; nothing in the passage ranks the work at all.

options.value: To show the Mole was bored and fed up with the climb.
To show the climb went on and on and was hard work.
To copy the sound of the birds singing up above.
To make the reader feel sorry for the Mole's sore arms.

stem.text: Read lines 17 to 19. Why did the birds' singing sound almost like a shout to the Mole?

carriers.key: He had been shut underground so long that his ears were not used to it.

options.value: The birds were much louder than usual that day.
The rabbits were shouting at him from the gap.
The hot sun made every sound seem bigger.
He had never heard a bird sing before in his life.
options.execution: 'Never heard a bird sing before in his life' is the absolute version of a true statement about his ears being out of practice.

options.value: He had been shut underground so long that his ears were not used to it.

stem.text: Read lines 23 to 27. What does the way the Mole treats the rabbits show about him?

carriers.key: He is so excited that he will not stop for anyone.

options.value: He is frightened of the older rabbit.
He is so excited that he will not stop for anyone.
He is a cruel animal who is always unkind.
options.execution: 'Always unkind' pushes one rush past a hedge into a permanent character.

options.value: He is rushing home to get his dinner.
He is sorry at once for knocking the rabbit over.

stem.text: The writer calls the river an animal that chases, chuckles and grips things. Read lines 29 to 33. Why does he do this?

carriers.key: To make the river seem alive, playful and always moving.

options.value: To make the river seem alive, playful and always moving.
Because a real animal was swimming in the water.
Because the river was dangerous and might grab the Mole.
options.execution: 'Gripping things' at line 30 is pushed to a threat; the passage's next words are 'with a gurgle' and 'leaving them with a laugh'.

options.value: Because the Water Rat lived in the bank beside it.
Because the Mole thought a big animal was in front of him.

stem.text: Lines 48 to 52 are four very short paragraphs. Each one adds one new detail. Why does the writer do this?

carriers.key: To let the reader see the face appear bit by bit, just as the Mole does.

options.value: To show that the Mole was creeping closer with every step.
To show that the Mole was afraid of the face.
To let the reader see the face appear bit by bit, just as the Mole does.
To copy the little jumps the Mole made across the meadow.
To make the face sound as grand as it possibly could be.
options.execution: 'As grand as it possibly could be' overstates a brown face with whiskers.

stem.text: The animals act like people, but we never forget they are animals. How does the writer do this?

carriers.key: He gives them houses, money and boats, but keeps their fur, paws and whiskers.

options.value: He keeps the animals quiet, still and dull, but lets the river chatter, gurgle and laugh.
He gives them human names, and leaves the animal ones behind.
He tells the reader, plainly and often, that these animals are really people.
He gives them houses, money and boats, but keeps their fur, paws and whiskers.
He makes every animal speak, move and think in exactly the same way.
options.execution: 'Exactly the same way' overstates: the rabbit charges a toll at line 22, the Rat sculls a boat at line 63, the Mole whitewashes a house at line 3.

stem.text: When Mr Darcy first walked in, the room thought very well of him. Read lines 26 to 30. Why?

carriers.key: Because of his looks, and because of the news that he was very rich.

options.value: Because he danced with lots of different ladies.
Because he spoke kindly to everyone he was introduced to.
Because he was the tallest man in the room.
options.execution: 'The tallest man in the room' is the absolute version of line 27's 'fine, tall person'.

options.value: Because of his looks, and because of the news that he was very rich.
Because he owned a large estate in Derbyshire.

stem.text: Halfway through the evening, people changed their minds about Mr Darcy. Read lines 30 to 35. What changed them?

carriers.key: The way he behaved, as if he were better than everyone there.

options.value: They found out that he was not really rich after all.
They decided he was less good-looking than Mr Bingley.
The way he behaved, as if he were better than everyone there.
He complained that the ball had ended too early.
Everybody disliked him from the moment he walked in.
options.execution: 'From the moment he walked in' overstates: line 30 has him admired for half the evening.

stem.text: Read lines 39 to 41. How many dances did Mr Darcy dance, and who did he dance with?

carriers.key: Two: one with Mrs Hurst and one with Miss Bingley.

options.value: Every dance of the evening.
Two: one with Mrs Hurst and one with Miss Bingley.
Two: one with Miss Bingley and one with Elizabeth.
None at all.
options.execution: 'None at all' is the absolute version of 'danced only once... and once' at lines 39 and 40.

options.value: Three: with Mrs Hurst, Miss Bingley and Miss Bennet.

stem.text: Read lines 41 to 43. The writer says: 'His character was decided. He was the proudest, most disagreeable man in the world.' What do these short, sure sentences do?

carriers.key: They make the room's quick opinion sound like a settled fact.

options.value: They prove that Mr Darcy really was the worst man alive.
options.execution: 'Really was the worst man alive' takes the room's verdict as the writer's own finding.

options.value: They show that the writer had run out of things to say about him.
They make the room's quick opinion sound like a settled fact.
They show that Mr Darcy had at last made up his mind about something.
They tell us that Mr Darcy said nothing to anybody all evening.

stem.text: Mrs Bennet disliked Mr Darcy more strongly than anybody else in the room did. Read lines 44 to 46. What made her feeling so strong?

carriers.key: He had been rude about one of her daughters.

options.value: He had been rude about one of her daughters.
He would not let anyone introduce him to her.
He had told Mr Bennet that he did not like the neighbourhood.
Mr Bingley had chosen to dance with her eldest daughter.
He was the proudest man in the world, and she hated proud people.
options.execution: 'The proudest man in the world' at line 42 is offered as her reason, which makes her feeling general when lines 45 and 46 make it particular.

stem.text: At the end, Elizabeth turns what happened into a story for her friends. Read lines 70 to 73. What does this tell us about her?

carriers.key: She can find the funny side of things, even when she has been treated badly.

options.value: She has completely forgiven Mr Darcy.
She can find the funny side of things, even when she has been treated badly.
She wants her friends to feel sorry for her.
What Mr Darcy said did not bother her at all.
options.execution: 'Did not bother her at all' overstates: line 70 says her feelings towards him were not cordial.

options.value: She thinks Mr Darcy is a fine, handsome man.

stem.text: Think about the whole passage. How do we learn what the people in it are like?

carriers.key: We are told what others say of them, but never whether the writer agrees.

options.value: We are told what the writer thinks, and not only what the room says.
We are shown what they do, but never told whether the writer approves.
We are given only Elizabeth's view, and no other opinion is ever allowed.
options.execution: Elizabeth does not appear until line 47 and gives no verdict at all; the opinions at lines 29, 42 and 44 belong to the room and to Mrs Bennet.

options.value: We are told what others say of them, but never whether the writer agrees.

stem.text: Read lines 33 to 46. The writer shows the girl to an 'ordinary observer', then to an 'extraordinary observer'. Why?

carriers.key: To show that there is far more to this girl than her plain looks suggest.

options.value: To show that the girl slowly changed while she sat there waiting for him.
To show that Matthew saw both of these things as he came down the platform.
To show that nobody could ever really know what this girl was like inside.
options.execution: Stretches to nobody and ever where the passage is measured.

options.value: To show that there is far more to this girl than her plain looks suggest.

stem.text: The girl says she had planned to sleep in a wild cherry-tree. What does this show about her? (lines 51 to 58)

carriers.key: She can turn a hard situation into something lovely.

options.value: She would rather sleep outside than go to Green Gables.
She can turn a hard situation into something lovely.
She is never frightened by anything at all.
options.execution: Stretches line 55; lines 51 and 52 say she was beginning to be afraid he was not coming.

options.value: She has slept outdoors many times before.

stem.text: Matthew decides to take the girl home. What does this decision show about him? (lines 59 to 63)

carriers.key: He would rather be kind now than face a hard talk.

options.value: Marilla had told him what to do in this case.
He never makes a decision by himself.
options.execution: Line 59 shows him deciding by himself, so never cannot hold.

options.value: He would rather be kind now than face a hard talk.
He had always hoped that a girl would come.

stem.text: The writer says 'would' again and again. He would shout, he would drop it, he would call us fools. What does that tell us about this day?

carriers.key: It is not one day at all, but what happened every single time.

options.value: It is not one clear memory, but a guess at what may have happened.
It tells us the picture was never hung, though he says it was.
options.execution: Stretches to never; line 58 has the picture up by midnight, crooked but up.

options.value: It tells us the story is remembered years after it all happened.
It is not one day at all, but what happened every single time.

stem.text: The trials sheet has eleven names and 'plenty of room left at the bottom'. Why does the writer tell us? (lines 37 to 39)

carriers.key: There is a space Reuben is not going to fill.

options.value: The football team still needs more players.
Reuben has already written his name on it.
Nobody at the school wants to play in September.
There is a space Reuben is not going to fill.

stem.text: Read lines 26 to 30, then lines 71 to 73. Why could the morning search never find the garden?

carriers.key: They searched round the house, but the garden lay behind the stables.

options.value: The house stood in a field, and no garden lay near it.
options.execution: Line 29 says no strip of garden touched the house, and line 72 finds the garden.

options.value: They had seen no wall at all, but only imagined it in the dark.
They searched round the house, but the garden lay behind the stables.
The garden had hidden itself away, and the high wall kept it out of sight.

stem.text: The writer keeps making one choice about the order she tells things in. Which is it?

carriers.key: We are shown the scene, but told the reason for it only afterwards.

options.value: She shows them creeping down to be useful, and then Mother wakes.
She lets Mother explain the whole of it, though the children had missed it.
We are told what the children do, but never what they feel.
options.execution: Line 11 gives Roberta's fun, line 39 their contentment, line 56 a wonderful breakfast.

options.value: We are shown the scene, but told the reason for it only afterwards.

stem.text: Read lines 4 and 5. What do they say about Saltmere and this walk?

carriers.key: He got as far as the caravan park, twice.

options.value: He got as far as Saltmere, twice.
He got as far as the caravan park, twice.
He had never set out for Saltmere before.
options.execution: Line 5 says twice, so never is stronger than the passage.

options.value: He walked out to Saltmere about four years ago.

stem.text: Read lines 10 to 12, then lines 33 to 35. What does standing on the step settle about Nan's story?

carriers.key: The story has two speeds, but the water he watches is the slow one.

options.value: The story has two speeds, but the water he watches is the slow one.
The sea took the whole row in one night in February, as she says.
None of what Nan has told him about the place ever really happened.
options.execution: Line 33 has him standing on the step, so at least that much of it is real.

options.value: The water comes up, but then leaves the step alone.

stem.text: Jane does the same thing again and again before describing something. What?

carriers.key: She reports the light first, but describes little beyond what it shows.

options.value: She tells us the sun sank down crimson and clear behind the trees.
She describes each person in full first, but gives their actions later.
She never describes a person, but only the weather and the sky.
options.execution: Lines 52 to 56 describe the traveller closely, from his cloak to his age.

options.value: She reports the light first, but describes little beyond what it shows.

stem.text: Mrs Umney offers the family a ghost story. How do they keep answering it?

carriers.key: They keep to household business, though she speaks of ghosts.

options.value: They keep saying, over and over, that the house has no ghost.
They laugh at her openly, while she is out of the room.
They never take her to heart, and answer her coldly.
options.execution: Line 54 has them answer her warmly, and line 57 leaves her better paid.

options.value: They keep to household business, though she speaks of ghosts.

stem.text: The writer keeps doing something the two children could not do. What?

carriers.key: He gives a children's quarrel, but explains it in grown-up words.

options.value: He tells us that Tom cut the puff and gave Maggie the best bit of it.
He takes Maggie's side, but keeps it out of his words.
He never once tells us what either child is feeling.
options.execution: Lines 33, 48 and 64 all give feelings the children never speak aloud.

options.value: He gives a children's quarrel, but explains it in grown-up words.

stem.text: Think about the whole passage. What does Dilan keep doing as he tells it?

carriers.key: He keeps saying it went well, but his own details say otherwise.

options.value: He says he is not in trouble, and his mother is behind the door.
He knows he went too far, but he keeps it from us.
He leaves out every single detail that could count against him.
options.execution: Every single is what defeats it; lines 28 to 34 report the damage.

options.value: He keeps saying it went well, but his own details say otherwise.
